value.body: A first officer is the co-pilot of an airliner, sharing flying and checklist duties with the captain. Airlines hire them for a specific aircraft type. A typical day involves flight planning, briefings, flying one or more sectors, and working within duty-time limits.

items.label: Licence needed
items.value: DGCA Commercial Pilot Licence (CPL) plus a type rating

items.label: Common aircraft
items.value: Narrow-body jets and turboprops on domestic routes

items.label: CPLs issued in a year
items.note: All CPLs, not only airline hires

value.title: How you get in
value.body: A Commercial Pilot Licence (CPL) from DGCA is the requirement, not a degree. It needs Class 12 with Physics and Maths (these can be added later through NIOS), a DGCA Class 1 medical, passes in the DGCA ground exams (Air Navigation, Meteorology, Air Regulations, Technical) plus a radio telephony licence, and about 200 hours of flying at a DGCA-approved flying school. Airlines then select pilots through tests and interviews, and a type rating on the aircraft (often paid for by the trainee) is needed before flying the line. Some airlines run cadet programmes that combine training and selection.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Crew coordination with the captain and cabin crew
Radio communication with air traffic control

value.title: At a glance
items: Training is expensive, and a CPL does not guarantee an airline job.
The usual next step is command (captain) after meeting hours and airline requirements.
Regular medicals and simulator checks continue throughout the career.
Schedules include early mornings, nights and holidays.
